title: Neovascular & Inflammatory Glaucoma: Clinical Management Guide
summary: An exhaustive clinical reference for Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) and Inflammatory Glaucoma variants. This guide covers pathophysiology, causative factors, diagnostic investigations, and multi-modal treatment strategies including anti-VEGF, PRP, and surgical interventions.

sections.title: Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG): Pathophysiology
sections.content: Posterior segment ischaemia drives neovascularization of the iris and drainage angle, leading to a fibrovascular membrane. Initially, this overlies the trabecular meshwork so that the angle appears open, but with time, PAS form and the membrane contracts to cause complete synechial angle closure. Ischaemic CrVO and diabetes each account for about a third of the cases of neovascular glaucoma (NVG). The advent of intravitreal anti-VEGF therapies have significantly helped in the management of early and refractory NVG. (Page 405)

sections.title: Comprehensive Etiology List
content: Ischaemic CrVO (common); risk of progression to NVG is 50%.
Diabetic retinopathy (common); risk of NVG highest in PDR.
Other vascular disorders: OIS, CrAO, BrVO.
Other retinal disease: chronic retinal detachment, sickle cell retinopathy.
Retinal or choroidal tumours.

branches: Pain: often severe; history of sudden vision loss months prior (e.g., CrVO)
Iris rubeosis: abnormal/non-radial vessels at pupil sphincter margin
High IOP; AC flare/cells; hyphaema; ectropion uvea
Conjunctival injection and corneal oedema (acute iIOP/decompensation)
Disc changes and field loss (as for POAG, pp. 390–1)
Gonioscopy: Abnormal vessels; fibrovascular membrane; PAS; synechial closure

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigations
content: Dilated fundoscopy in all cases ± FFA to determine cause.
Carotid Doppler US: if no retinal pathology or asymmetric diabetic retinopathy.
B-scan US: if poor fundal view (cataract associated with tumours, detachment, inflammation).
Haematological/biochemical factors: factors increasing hypoxic drive, e.g., anaemia.

sections.title: NVG Treatment: Underlying Cause
content: PRP for retinal ischaemia.
Retinal reattachment for retinal detachment.
Carotid endarterectomy for suitable carotid artery stenosis.
Treat exacerbating factors: e.g., anaemia, hyperviscosity.

sections.title: Management of Neovascularization
sections.content:
Treatment is undergoing a positive transformation with anti-VEGF. Note: anti-VEGF alone will not control NVG unless posterior hypoxic drive is addressed (PRP, etc). PRP decreases long-term drive. If no fundal view, anti-VEGF temporizes. Consider Vitrectomy/endolaser ± cataract extraction based on prognosis. Anti-VEGF improves drainage surgery survival. Intravitreal bevacizumab shows regression of NV and decreased IOP alone [6] or with PRP [7].

6: Wakabayashi t et al. Ophthalmology. 2008;115:1571–80.
7: Ehlers JP et al. Retina. 2008;28:696–702.

rows: IOP & Inflammation
Cycloplegic (Atropine 1% 2x/d); Topical steroids (Pred acetate 1% 1-4hrly); Ocular hypotensives (as for POAG). Surgical: Augmented trabeculectomy, tube-shunt, or cyclodiode.
Pain Management
Cycloplegia (atropine) and topical corticosteroids; Lubricants for sick epithelium (suspicion for microbial keratitis); Full surface regime for dry eyes/blepharitis/toxicity.
Blind & Painful Eye
Retrobulbar alcohol or chlorpromazine; Evisceration or enucleation.

sections.title: Inflammatory Glaucoma: General Principles
sections.content: Raised IOP in intraocular inflammation is common. Challenges: elucidating time course (acute vs chronic iIOP), angle state (open vs appositional vs synechial), and mechanism. Therapy is difficult due to IOP fluctuations (ciliary body shutdown lowers IOP; trabeculitis increases IOP) and concerns regarding steroid-induced glaucoma. (Page 406-407)

rows: Acute
Acute trabeculitis (HSV, VZV), TM blockage.
iIOP; open angle; signs of uveitis ± keratitis; IOP returns to normal after episode.
Inflammatory process: Topical steroids/cycloplegics (as for AAU, pp. 460-1). IOP: if >27mmHg, sustained, or vulnerable disc, use topical (β-blocker, CAI) or systemic (acetazolamide).
Chronic
Trabecular scarring; chronic trabeculitis.
iIOP; open angle; no active inflammation but signs of previous episodes; ± disc/field defects (p. 384); Sectorial iris atrophy.
Medical: as for POAG. Avoid PGAs (risk of herpetic reactivation). Surgical: Augmented trabeculectomy (tight inflammation control first) or tube. Cyclodestruction risk: Phthisis.

sections.title: Steroid-Induced Glaucoma
content: Important differential for inflammatory glaucoma.
If due to steroids: reduce potency/frequency ± steroid-sparing agents.
If due to inflammation: steroid dose may need to be increased.
IOP elevation may be dose-dependent.

rows: With Seclusio Pupillae
360° PS blocks aqueous flow; iris bombé; appositional closure.
Features: Iris bombé; shallow AC. Tx: Minimize PS (subconjunctival Betnesol®/mydricaine). Nd:YAG PI (large/multiple); surgical PI if needed. Topical/systemic IOP meds.
With Synechial Closure
PAS lead to closure; risk increases in granulomatous inflammation/narrow angles.
Features: PAS; signs of previous inflammation. Tx: Medical (caution with PGAs); Augmented trabeculectomy or tube (risk of hypotony); Cyclodiode (risk of phthisis). Ensure patent PI.

content.explanation: Painless unilateral recurrent high IOP episodes in a 'white' eye. Typically young males. Postulated HSV trabeculitis.

sections.title: PSS Clinical & Treatment
content: Features: Blurring, haloes, high IOP (40–80mmHg), minimal flare, white eye, occasional cells/KPs, NO synechiae, open angle.
Treatment: Topical steroid (dexamethasone 0.1% 4x/d); Topical IOP meds (β-blocker, α2-agonist, CAI) or systemic acetazolamide.
NB: Recurrent episodes may lead to severe angle damage.

sections.title: Fuchs’ Heterochromic Uveitis
content: Syndrome of mild chronic anterior uveitis, iris heterochromia, and cataract.
Glaucoma occurs in 10–30% of cases. Typically affects young adults; unilateral in >90%.
Strong association with the rubella virus.
Symptoms: dVA (cataract), floaters; often asymptomatic.

Signs: White eye, white stellate KPs (whole endothelium), mild flare/few cells, iris atrophy (moth-eaten), transillumination defects, abnormal iris vessels, iris heterochromia (becomes bluer), iris nodules, vitritis, iIOP.
Gonioscopy: Open angle; ± twig-like neovascularization of the angle (NVA).
Treatment: Inflammatory process tx usually unnecessary. iIOP treated as for POAG (pp. 390–1).
